The emotional arc is striking: you started Monday with lower energy and a work handover, and ended Friday sunburnt on floaties calling it 'really really great day.' The Japan leg closed beautifully — and Bora Bora delivered something quieter and deeper.

moments.body: You wrote this the morning after — which says something. Michelin dinner, matcha, Golden Gai cocktails, Shibuya crossing, an arcade, onsen, and a sake tasting where you ended up chatting with a high-ranking member of the Japanese air defense. Golden Gai's maze of 200 tiny bars in Shinjuku is one of Tokyo's great surprises — each fits maybe eight people, and the conversations that happen there are exactly the kind you described. A crystalline honeymoon memory.
moments.title: The Perfect Tokyo Day (Recap)

moments.body: Tennis with Dave, a run, weights, Gremly progress, alcohol avoided — all before you described yourself as 'very very refreshed.' You wondered if the long sleep helped. Bora Bora's heat and the shift from three weeks of pre-honeymoon compression likely played a role too. This was the week's integration peak: every domain working at once, none crowding the others out.
moments.title: Very Very Refreshed

moments.body: 'More sun burnt than I want to be but it feels like a big dose of vitamin D did me good.' The Bora Bora lagoon's turquoise clarity and equatorial sun hit differently after a British winter and a San Francisco grey spell. Spending the afternoon on the floaties with Dave — not planning, not building, just being — was the quiet counterpoint to March 8's productivity peak. Both days were great. They were great differently.

spotlight.title: High stimulation pauses your inner work
spotlight.takeaway: When life is externally rich, the internal practices are easiest to skip — and hardest to notice you've skipped. The habit may resume naturally when you're back in San Francisco, but it's worth watching whether it returns on its own.
spotlight.evidence_trail: The 'Stop negative thoughts' habit has averaged 43% completion across its full tracking window (9/21 days). This week: 0 completions across 7 days — the first complete drop since the habit began. What changed? The external environment shifted dramatically: Tokyo sensory overload (March 2), Kyoto travel (March 3), Bora Bora arrival (March 6), poolside cabana, tennis, jet skiing, floaties. Meanwhile, your journal mood tags were overwhelmingly positive — grateful, great, hopeful — with no anxiety or stress entries. The practice wasn't needed in the way it usually is. But it also wasn't practiced.

research_context.body: Novelty and high-reward environments flood the brain's attentional systems, making inward-facing practices feel less salient — not because they're unneeded, but because the signal that usually triggers them (low mood, rumination) is temporarily absent. For people who use structured habits to manage their inner state, high-stimulation travel can create a 'false floor' — things feel fine, so the scaffolding quietly disappears. The risk isn't this week. It's the week after you land back in Cole Valley.

cards.body: The first week of March answered a question that's been building since January: what happens to all your threads when you're fully immersed in something extraordinary? Most held. Strength training survived three destination changes. Sobriety held in Bora Bora. Gremly kept moving. What slipped — running, negative thought tracking — slipped quietly, without drama. The month is young, but the pattern is already clear: you carry more with you than most people do.
